questions.stem:
A microbiology lab tests a panel of drugs against two reference organisms grown under the conditions each prefers. Organism 1 is an obligate aerobe, and organism 2 is an obligate anaerobe. Drug P kills organism 2 but has no effect on organism 1, even at high concentrations and even though organism 1 has never been exposed to it. Neither organism carries plasmids or resistance genes.

Which drug is P most likely, and why does organism 1 resist it?
choices: Metronidazole, because the aerobe cannot reduce the drug to its active form
Gentamicin, because the aerobe lacks the oxidative metabolism to take it up
Vancomycin, because the aerobe's outer membrane keeps the drug from its target
Aztreonam, because the aerobe's penicillin-binding proteins do not bind it
Ceftriaxone, because the aerobe produces a chromosomal carbapenemase

explain.html:
Intrinsic resistance is the innate ability of a species to resist an antibiotic because of its normal structural or functional characteristics, in contrast to resistance acquired by gene transfer. The lecture gives a set of examples. Aerobic bacteria resist metronidazole because they cannot anaerobically reduce the drug to its active form. Anaerobes resist aminoglycosides because they lack the oxidative metabolism to take the drug up. Vancomycin cannot get through the Gram-negative envelope, and aztreonam cannot treat Gram-positives because their penicillin-binding proteins do not bind it.

Here the decisive finding is the direction of the result: drug P kills the anaerobe and spares the aerobe, with no plasmids or resistance genes in either. Only metronidazole depends on anaerobic metabolism for activation, so the aerobe resists it by nature. These examples explain much of the coverage pattern of each drug.
explain.table:
DrugIntrinsically resistant groupReason
MetronidazoleAerobesCannot reduce the drug to its active form
AminoglycosidesAnaerobesNo oxidative metabolism to take up the drug
VancomycinGram-negativesCannot penetrate the outer membrane
AztreonamGram-positivesTheir PBPs do not bind it
why: Aminoglycoside uptake needs oxidative metabolism, so they kill aerobes and spare anaerobes, the reverse of this result.
The vancomycin barrier is the Gram-negative outer membrane, which has nothing to do with oxygen use.
Aztreonam fails against Gram-positives because their PBPs do not bind it, not because of aerobic metabolism.
A carbapenemase is an acquired enzyme, and the stem rules out resistance genes.
explain.takeaway: Aerobic bacteria are intrinsically resistant to metronidazole because they cannot reduce it to its active form, while anaerobes are intrinsically resistant to aminoglycosides because they cannot take them up.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Recognize intrinsic resistance as a normal structural or functional trait of a bacterial species, as distinct from acquired resistance.

rows.why: Aminoglycoside uptake needs oxidative metabolism, so they kill aerobes and spare anaerobes, the reverse of this result.
rows.if_right: a drug that kills the aerobe and has no effect on the anaerobe

rows.why: The vancomycin barrier is the Gram-negative outer membrane, which has nothing to do with oxygen use.
rows.if_right: an organism that resists the drug because it is Gram-negative

rows.why: Aztreonam fails against Gram-positives because their PBPs do not bind it, not because of aerobic metabolism.
rows.if_right: a Gram-positive organism that resists a monobactam

rows.why: A carbapenemase is an acquired enzyme, and the stem rules out resistance genes.
rows.if_right: an isolate carrying a plasmid-encoded beta-lactamase

questions.stem:
A 72-year-old woman in a long-term care facility with an indwelling urinary catheter develops urosepsis. Urine and blood grow a lactose-fermenting, encapsulated Gram-negative rod that is resistant to imipenem, meropenem and ertapenem. Molecular testing shows two changes: a gene for an enzyme that hydrolyzes all beta-lactams, and reduced production of outer membrane channel proteins.

How does the second change contribute to resistance?
choices: It alters the penicillin-binding proteins so the drug no longer binds
It adds acetyl groups to the drug so that it no longer binds its target
It actively pumps the drug from the cytoplasm back out of the cell
It slows passive entry of the drug across the outer membrane
It replaces terminal D-alanine with D-lactate in the cell wall precursors

explain.html:
Carbapenems are bactericidal beta-lactams that must reach their penicillin-binding proteins to work. In Gram-negatives that means crossing the outer membrane through porins, beta-barrel channels through which beta-lactams passively diffuse. Enterobacteriaceae resist carbapenems by two mechanisms: alteration or reduction of porins, which keeps drug out, and production of a carbapenemase such as KPC, which hydrolyzes all beta-lactams. The CDC defines CRE as Enterobacteriaceae resistant to any carbapenem and documented to produce a carbapenemase.

An encapsulated, lactose-fermenting Gram-negative rod causing catheter-associated urosepsis in a nursing home resident, resistant to every carbapenem, is CRE, most likely Klebsiella. Its second change, fewer outer membrane channels, slows passive drug entry, and the enzyme destroys whatever does get in. Patients with catheters and ventilators are the ones most at risk.
why: Altered PBPs are a resistance mechanism, but the stem describes fewer outer membrane channels, not a changed target.
Adding acetyl groups describes aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes, not a porin change.
Efflux pumps actively expel drug, whereas porins are passive entry channels.
D-Ala-D-Lac precursors are the vancomycin resistance mechanism of VRE, unrelated to carbapenems.
explain.takeaway: Enterobacteriaceae resist carbapenems by producing carbapenemases such as KPC and by reducing or altering the outer membrane porins through which beta-lactams diffuse to their PBPs.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Explain the two mechanisms of carbapenem resistance employed by Enterobacteriaceae.

rows.why: Altered PBPs are a resistance mechanism, but the stem describes fewer outer membrane channels, not a changed target.
rows.if_right: a mutation that lowers carbapenem binding to penicillin-binding proteins

rows.why: Adding acetyl groups describes aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes, not a porin change.
rows.if_right: an aminoglycoside recovered from culture carrying new acetyl groups

rows.why: Efflux pumps actively expel drug, whereas porins are passive entry channels.
rows.if_right: a transporter that removes drug and whose blockade restores susceptibility

rows.why: D-Ala-D-Lac precursors are the vancomycin resistance mechanism of VRE, unrelated to carbapenems.
rows.if_right: vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium

questions.stem:
A hospital lab tests a urinary Klebsiella isolate.

[[labs 0]]

Which enzyme best explains this pattern?
choices: A penicillinase that hydrolyzes only penicillins
A metallo-beta-lactamase that requires zinc
An extended-spectrum beta-lactamase
A carbapenemase such as KPC
An altered penicillin-binding protein 2a

explain.html:
Beta-lactamases hydrolyze the beta-lactam ring, and they are grouped by what they destroy. Penicillinases destroy penicillins. Extended-spectrum beta-lactamases (ESBLs) confer resistance to penicillins, cephalosporins and the monobactam aztreonam and can be inhibited by clavulanic acid, tazobactam or sulbactam. Carbapenemases confer resistance to all of those plus the carbapenems.

This isolate fails ampicillin, ceftriaxone, cefepime and aztreonam, which is already beyond a penicillinase. It stays susceptible to meropenem, which excludes a carbapenemase, and clavulanate restores activity, which fits an ESBL exactly. Spotting carbapenem susceptibility plus inhibitor rescue is the quickest way to call an ESBL.
why: A penicillinase would leave ceftriaxone, cefepime and aztreonam active.
Metallo-beta-lactamases are carbapenemases and would make meropenem fail.
A carbapenemase such as KPC would hydrolyze meropenem too.
PBP2a is the S. aureus target change in MRSA, not a Gram-negative enzyme, and inhibitors would not rescue it.
explain.takeaway: ESBLs hydrolyze penicillins, cephalosporins and aztreonam, are inhibited by clavulanate, tazobactam or sulbactam, and leave carbapenems active.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Explain the two mechanisms of carbapenem resistance employed by Enterobacteriaceae.

rows.why: A penicillinase would leave ceftriaxone, cefepime and aztreonam active.
rows.if_right: resistance to ampicillin only, with cephalosporins and aztreonam still active

rows.why: Metallo-beta-lactamases are carbapenemases and would make meropenem fail.
rows.if_right: an isolate resistant to meropenem whose enzyme needs zinc

rows.why: A carbapenemase such as KPC would hydrolyze meropenem too.
rows.if_right: meropenem resistance in a Klebsiella isolate

rows.why: PBP2a is the S. aureus target change in MRSA, not a Gram-negative enzyme, and inhibitors would not rescue it.
rows.if_right: an oxacillin-resistant S. aureus isolate

questions.stem:
A 64-year-old man on a ventilator develops pneumonia. Sputum grows Klebsiella pneumoniae that is resistant to all carbapenems and is documented to produce a Klebsiella pneumoniae carbapenemase. Susceptibility testing shows the isolate remains susceptible to a newer combination of a beta-lactam with a beta-lactamase inhibitor.

Which agent is that combination?
choices: Amoxicillin-clavulanate
Ampicillin-sulbactam
Piperacillin-tazobactam
Imipenem-cilastatin
Ceftazidime-avibactam

explain.html:
Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae leave very few choices, and the choice rests on detailed susceptibility testing. Options are often limited to tigecycline, fosfomycin and aminoglycosides (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin). Two newer FDA-approved drugs pair a beta-lactam with a beta-lactamase inhibitor: ceftazidime-avibactam (Avycaz) and meropenem-vaborbactam (Vabomere). These newer combinations are the ones built for this problem.

The isolate is a documented KPC producer resistant to every carbapenem, and testing shows susceptibility to a newer beta-lactam/inhibitor combination. Of the choices, only ceftazidime-avibactam is on that list. The older combinations are not CRE treatments, and imipenem-cilastatin is a carbapenem the enzyme already destroys.
why: Amoxicillin-clavulanate is an older combination and is not among the CRE treatments listed.
Ampicillin-sulbactam is an older combination and is not a listed CRE option.
Piperacillin-tazobactam is not among the CRE options, which name avibactam and vaborbactam combinations.
Cilastatin blocks renal dehydropeptidase rather than beta-lactamases, and imipenem is hydrolyzed by the carbapenemase.
explain.takeaway: CRE treatment is limited to tigecycline, fosfomycin, aminoglycosides and newer beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor combinations such as ceftazidime-avibactam and meropenem-vaborbactam.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Know how to treat each resistant infection (responsible for drugs highlighted in red).

rows.why: Amoxicillin-clavulanate is an older combination and is not among the CRE treatments listed.
rows.if_right: an ESBL-producing or penicillinase-producing isolate without a carbapenemase

rows.why: Ampicillin-sulbactam is an older combination and is not a listed CRE option.
rows.if_right: an isolate whose only enzyme is a penicillinase or ESBL

rows.why: Piperacillin-tazobactam is not among the CRE options, which name avibactam and vaborbactam combinations.
rows.if_right: empiric two-class coverage for suspected MDR Pseudomonas, paired with an aminoglycoside

rows.why: Cilastatin blocks renal dehydropeptidase rather than beta-lactamases, and imipenem is hydrolyzed by the carbapenemase.
rows.if_right: a carbapenem-susceptible isolate, where imipenem needs cilastatin to avoid renal inactivation

questions.stem:
A 22-year-old college wrestler has a tender, fluctuant, draining abscess on his thigh. Two teammates had similar lesions. After incision and drainage, culture grows Gram-positive cocci in clusters that are coagulase positive and resistant to oxacillin. He is well appearing and afebrile and will be treated at home.

Which oral antibiotic is an appropriate choice?
choices: Dicloxacillin
Cephalexin
Amoxicillin-clavulanate
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole
Vancomycin capsules taken by mouth

explain.html:
MRSA is resistant to all beta-lactams because of PBP2a, so beta-lactam choices are off the table no matter which inhibitor is added. Vancomycin is the first-choice drug for serious MRSA infection, with daptomycin, linezolid and tigecycline as other options. For home use, the oral drugs are trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, clindamycin, minocycline and doxycycline. Community-acquired MRSA is favored by crowded living and athletics, and its skin infections present as tender, swollen lumps that drain pus.

A draining thigh abscess in a wrestler whose teammates had the same lesions, growing coagulase-positive cocci in clusters that resist oxacillin, is community-acquired MRSA. He is well and going home, so an oral MRSA agent fits, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is on that list.
why: Dicloxacillin is an anti-staphylococcal penicillin, and MRSA resists every beta-lactam through PBP2a.
Cephalexin is a cephalosporin, and MRSA resists all beta-lactams.
Clavulanate blocks the PC1 penicillinase but cannot overcome PBP2a.
Oral vancomycin is not the home MRSA option; vancomycin for MRSA is the first-choice intravenous drug for serious infection.
explain.takeaway: Vancomycin is first choice for serious MRSA infection, oral home options are trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, clindamycin, doxycycline and minocycline, and all beta-lactams fail because of PBP2a.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Know how to treat each resistant infection (responsible for drugs highlighted in red).

rows.why: Dicloxacillin is an anti-staphylococcal penicillin, and MRSA resists every beta-lactam through PBP2a.
rows.if_right: an oxacillin-susceptible (MSSA) skin infection

rows.why: Cephalexin is a cephalosporin, and MRSA resists all beta-lactams.
rows.if_right: an MSSA skin infection treated at home

rows.why: Clavulanate blocks the PC1 penicillinase but cannot overcome PBP2a.
rows.if_right: a S. aureus isolate whose only resistance is the PC1 penicillinase

rows.why: Oral vancomycin is not the home MRSA option; vancomycin for MRSA is the first-choice intravenous drug for serious infection.
rows.if_right: a hospitalized patient with serious MRSA infection given vancomycin intravenously

questions.stem:
A 59-year-old woman with a long hospital stay develops a urinary catheter-associated bacteremia. Blood cultures grow Enterococcus faecium that is resistant to vancomycin and to ampicillin. She has no lung involvement.

Which drug is an appropriate treatment option for this infection?
choices: Ceftriaxone
Daptomycin
Aztreonam
Cefazolin
Clindamycin

explain.html:
VRE infections are hard to treat because enterococci are intrinsically resistant to many classes, including beta-lactams through low-affinity PBPs, low levels of aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, trimethoprim and clindamycin, and they acquire resistance to many others. The approach is to use ampicillin first if the isolate is susceptible. Otherwise the options are daptomycin, linezolid, tigecycline and eravacycline. Enterococci cause UTIs, bacteremia and endocarditis as opportunistic hospital pathogens.

This catheter-associated bacteremia grows E. faecium resistant to both vancomycin and ampicillin, so the first-choice drug is gone. Daptomycin is one of the listed alternatives and fits. None of the other choices has reliable enterococcal activity.
why: Enterococci are intrinsically resistant to beta-lactams such as cephalosporins.
Aztreonam cannot treat Gram-positive infections because their PBPs do not bind it.
Cefazolin is a cephalosporin, and enterococci resist beta-lactams through low-affinity PBPs.
Enterococci are intrinsically resistant to clindamycin.
explain.takeaway: VRE is treated with ampicillin if susceptible, and otherwise with daptomycin, linezolid, tigecycline or eravacycline.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Know how to treat each resistant infection (responsible for drugs highlighted in red).

rows.why: Enterococci are intrinsically resistant to beta-lactams such as cephalosporins.
rows.if_right: a cephalosporin-susceptible Gram-negative bacteremia

rows.why: Aztreonam cannot treat Gram-positive infections because their PBPs do not bind it.
rows.if_right: a Gram-negative rod bacteremia in a patient with penicillin allergy

rows.why: Cefazolin is a cephalosporin, and enterococci resist beta-lactams through low-affinity PBPs.
rows.if_right: an MSSA bacteremia

rows.why: Enterococci are intrinsically resistant to clindamycin.
rows.if_right: an anaerobic or MRSA skin infection

questions.stem:
Researchers sequence a multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii isolate that is resistant to ciprofloxacin and trimethoprim. They find point mutations in two chromosomal genes. Purified enzyme from each mutant gene still carries out its normal reaction at nearly normal rates, but each drug now binds its enzyme far less tightly.

Which two genes are most likely mutated?
choices: Penicillin-binding protein and porin genes
30S ribosomal protein and efflux pump genes
DNA gyrase and dihydrofolate reductase genes
Dihydropteroate synthase and RNA polymerase genes
Beta-lactamase and aminoglycoside-modifying enzyme genes

explain.html:
One resistance strategy is to change the drug's target. In A. baumannii, point mutations in DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV decrease or eliminate fluoroquinolone binding, and mutations in dihydrofolate reductase cause trimethoprim resistance. The key principle is that these mutations significantly reduce drug binding while mildly or not at all affecting enzyme activity. The bacterium keeps the function and loses the vulnerability.

The stem describes exactly that: two chromosomal point mutations, each enzyme still working at near-normal rates, each drug binding far less tightly. Ciprofloxacin targets DNA gyrase and trimethoprim targets dihydrofolate reductase, so those are the two genes. The same target-site strategy appears in MDR Pseudomonas.
explain.table:
DrugResistance in MDR-AB and MDR-PA
AminoglycosidesAMEs (main), rRNA modification, efflux
Beta-lactamsLow-affinity PBPs, beta-lactamases, porin loss, efflux
FluoroquinolonesMutations in DNA gyrase or topoisomerase IV
TrimethoprimMutation of dihydrofolate reductase
why: PBP and porin changes cause beta-lactam resistance, not fluoroquinolone or trimethoprim resistance.
Neither drug acts at the 30S subunit, and efflux pumps are transporters rather than mutated drug targets.
Dihydropteroate synthase is the sulfonamide target, and neither drug targets RNA polymerase.
Beta-lactamases and AMEs destroy or modify drugs rather than being altered targets.
explain.takeaway: Point mutations that lower drug binding but preserve enzyme function cause fluoroquinolone resistance (DNA gyrase, topoisomerase IV) and trimethoprim resistance (dihydrofolate reductase).
explain.topic: Target site mutations: fluoroquinolones and trimethoprim
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Explain the various strategies used by A. baumannii and P. aeruginosa to become resistant to aminoglycosides, beta-lactams, trimethoprim, and fluoroquinolones.

rows.why: PBP and porin changes cause beta-lactam resistance, not fluoroquinolone or trimethoprim resistance.
rows.if_right: an isolate resistant to carbapenems through low-affinity PBPs and porin loss

rows.why: Neither drug acts at the 30S subunit, and efflux pumps are transporters rather than mutated drug targets.
rows.if_right: an aminoglycoside-resistant isolate with rRNA changes and overexpressed pumps

rows.why: Dihydropteroate synthase is the sulfonamide target, and neither drug targets RNA polymerase.
rows.if_right: resistance to sulfamethoxazole plus a transcription inhibitor

rows.why: Beta-lactamases and AMEs destroy or modify drugs rather than being altered targets.
rows.if_right: resistance caused by enzymes that chemically inactivate beta-lactams and aminoglycosides

questions.stem:
A hospital lab reports an Acinetobacter baumannii isolate tested against seven standard antimicrobial categories for this organism. It is non-susceptible to at least one agent in each of these categories: aminoglycosides, antipseudomonal penicillins with inhibitors, cephalosporins, carbapenems, fluoroquinolones and folate inhibitors. It remains susceptible to the agents in one category, the glycylcyclines (tigecycline).

How should this isolate be classified?
choices: Susceptible, because one category still works
Multidrug resistant but not extensively drug resistant
Intrinsically resistant
Pan-drug resistant
Extensively drug resistant

explain.html:
Resistance in organisms like A. baumannii is graded by how many antimicrobial categories still work. Multidrug resistant (MDR) means acquired non-susceptibility to at least one agent in three or more categories. Extensively drug resistant (XDR) means non-susceptibility to at least one agent in all but two or fewer categories, so only one or two categories remain active. Pan-drug resistant (PDR) means non-susceptibility to all agents in all categories.

This isolate fails six of seven categories and remains susceptible only to tigecycline, so it is XDR. It technically also meets the MDR threshold, but XDR is the more specific label. Tigecycline is often the last option against carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter.
explain.table:
LabelDefinitionCategories still active
MDRNon-susceptible in 3 or more categoriesPossibly many
XDRNon-susceptible in all but 2 or fewer1 or 2
PDRNon-susceptible in all categoriesNone
why: Non-susceptibility in six categories is far beyond a susceptible isolate.
It exceeds the MDR threshold, and with only one category left the more specific label is XDR.
This is acquired resistance across many classes, not a normal trait of the species.
PDR requires non-susceptibility to every agent in every category, and tigecycline still works.
explain.takeaway: MDR is non-susceptibility in 3 or more categories, XDR leaves only 1 or 2 categories active, and PDR is non-susceptibility to all categories.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Recognize CRE, VRE, MRSA, MDR-AB and MDR-PA infections based on laboratory findings and disease presentation.

rows.why: Non-susceptibility in six categories is far beyond a susceptible isolate.
rows.if_right: an isolate non-susceptible in no categories

rows.why: It exceeds the MDR threshold, and with only one category left the more specific label is XDR.
rows.if_right: non-susceptibility in three categories with several others still active

rows.why: This is acquired resistance across many classes, not a normal trait of the species.
rows.if_right: a species that never responds to a drug because of its structure, such as aerobes and metronidazole

rows.why: PDR requires non-susceptibility to every agent in every category, and tigecycline still works.
rows.if_right: an isolate also non-susceptible to tigecycline, leaving no active category

questions.stem:
A carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii isolate is also resistant to fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines, erythromycin and tigecycline. When researchers add an experimental compound that blocks a tripartite membrane transporter spanning the inner membrane, periplasm and outer membrane, the minimum inhibitory concentrations of all of these unrelated drugs fall together.

Which resistance mechanism does this experiment reveal?
choices: A single enzyme that hydrolyzes all of these drug classes at once
Overexpressed multidrug efflux pumps that expel the drugs
Low-affinity penicillin-binding proteins that ignore the drugs
Loss of porins that these drugs need to cross the outer membrane
Point mutations in one shared ribosomal target of these drugs

explain.html:
Efflux pumps remove drug from the cytoplasm or periplasm and lower its effective concentration inside the cell. Overproduction of multidrug efflux pumps is common in A. baumannii, and the pumps span the inner membrane, periplasm and outer membrane. One pump handles many structurally unrelated drugs: aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines, chloramphenicol, erythromycin, trimethoprim and tigecycline. Pump overexpression also contributes to beta-lactam resistance in this organism.

The experiment shows the signature of efflux: resistance to several unrelated classes falls together when one membrane-spanning transporter is blocked. No single enzyme or target change could do that. That is why efflux pump inhibitors are a proposed future strategy.
why: No single enzyme destroys fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines, erythromycin and tigecycline; beta-lactamases act on beta-lactams.
Low-affinity PBPs affect beta-lactams only, and none of these drugs binds PBPs.
Porin loss limits entry, and blocking an export transporter would not reverse it.
These drugs have different targets (gyrase, 30S, 50S), so one shared target mutation is impossible.
explain.takeaway: MDR Acinetobacter overexpresses multidrug efflux pumps that expel aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines, erythromycin, trimethoprim and tigecycline.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Explain the various strategies used by A. baumannii and P. aeruginosa to become resistant to aminoglycosides, beta-lactams, trimethoprim, and fluoroquinolones.

rows.why: No single enzyme destroys fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines, erythromycin and tigecycline; beta-lactamases act on beta-lactams.
rows.if_right: resistance limited to beta-lactams that falls with a beta-lactamase inhibitor

rows.why: Low-affinity PBPs affect beta-lactams only, and none of these drugs binds PBPs.
rows.if_right: carbapenem resistance in A. baumannii from low-affinity PBPs

rows.why: Porin loss limits entry, and blocking an export transporter would not reverse it.
rows.if_right: carbapenem resistance in a Klebsiella isolate with fewer porins

rows.why: These drugs have different targets (gyrase, 30S, 50S), so one shared target mutation is impossible.
rows.if_right: resistance to a single drug class from a point mutation in its target

questions.stem:
Two Staphylococcus aureus isolates are compared. Isolate 1 is resistant to penicillin but susceptible to oxacillin, cefazolin and amoxicillin-clavulanate. Isolate 2 is resistant to penicillin, oxacillin, cefazolin, amoxicillin-clavulanate and meropenem. Both carry a plasmid-borne transposon encoding the same enzyme, but only isolate 2 carries a second, chromosomal gene.

What does the second gene in isolate 2 encode, and why does it defeat even inhibitor combinations?
choices: A penicillin-binding protein whose active site is shielded from typical beta-lactams
A carbapenemase that hydrolyzes every beta-lactam, even inhibitor-protected ones
An efflux pump that removes beta-lactams from the periplasm before they act
A ligase that makes D-alanyl-D-lactate precursors the drugs cannot bind
A porin mutation that keeps beta-lactams from crossing the outer membrane

explain.html:
S. aureus has two main mechanisms of beta-lactam resistance. The first is PC1, a penicillinase carried on a transposon located on a plasmid, nearly ubiquitous in staphylococci and susceptible to beta-lactamase inhibitors. The second is acquisition of the mecA gene encoding PBP2a, a modified penicillin-binding protein with an extra loop that blocks the transpeptidase active site from molecules the size of typical beta-lactams while leaving normal enzyme function intact. MRSA describes strains resistant to all beta-lactams.

Isolate 1 has only PC1: penicillin fails, but oxacillin, cefazolin and amoxicillin-clavulanate work, so it is MSSA. Isolate 2 also carries the chromosomal mecA and resists everything, including meropenem. Because the problem is the target and not an enzyme, adding an inhibitor cannot help.
explain.table:
PC1 penicillinasePBP2a (mecA)
TypeEnzyme that destroys penicillinAltered target with a shielded active site
LocationTransposon on a plasmidChromosomal cassette
Inhibitor rescueYesNo
ResultPenicillin resistant (MSSA)All beta-lactams resistant (MRSA)
why: Carbapenemases are a Gram-negative (CRE) mechanism, not how MRSA resists beta-lactams.
Staphylococci have no outer membrane or periplasm, and efflux is not one of the two MRSA mechanisms.
D-Ala-D-Lac precursors cause vancomycin resistance, not beta-lactam resistance.
S. aureus is Gram-positive and has no outer membrane porins.
explain.takeaway: S. aureus resists beta-lactams with the plasmid-borne PC1 penicillinase, which inhibitors block, and with mecA-encoded PBP2a, an altered target that makes MRSA resistant to all beta-lactams.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Describe the two mechanisms of beta-lactam resistance found in MRSA.

rows.why: Carbapenemases are a Gram-negative (CRE) mechanism, not how MRSA resists beta-lactams.
rows.if_right: a carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella that produces KPC

rows.why: Staphylococci have no outer membrane or periplasm, and efflux is not one of the two MRSA mechanisms.
rows.if_right: multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter expelling several drug classes

rows.why: D-Ala-D-Lac precursors cause vancomycin resistance, not beta-lactam resistance.
rows.if_right: an isolate that resists vancomycin but not beta-lactams

rows.why: S. aureus is Gram-positive and has no outer membrane porins.
rows.if_right: a Gram-negative rod with reduced porin expression

questions.stem:
A 68-year-old man in the intensive care unit for 3 weeks, who has received long courses of vancomycin and cephalosporins, develops bacteremia. Blood cultures grow Gram-positive cocci in pairs and short chains that are catalase negative, gamma-hemolytic and grow in 6.5% sodium chloride. The isolate is E. faecium. Vancomycin MIC is far above the susceptible range.

Which change in this organism best explains its resistance to the drug he was receiving?
choices: Production of a beta-lactamase that hydrolyzes the drug
Mutation of PBP2a so that the drug cannot reach the active site
Peptidoglycan precursors ending in D-alanyl-D-lactate
Aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes that acetylate the drug
Loss of outer membrane porins that the drug uses for entry

explain.html:
Vancomycin works by binding the D-Ala-D-Ala end of the peptidoglycan precursor and blocking transpeptidation. VRE carry a gene cluster that builds D-Ala-D-Lac instead and incorporates it into the wall, which causes a 1,000-fold decrease in vancomycin binding. Cell wall synthesis continues normally with the altered precursor, so the organism loses nothing. E. faecalis is more pathogenic, but E. faecium is more resistant and accounts for most VRE.

Enterococci are Gram-positive cocci in pairs or short chains, gamma-hemolytic, and identified by tolerance of 6.5% NaCl. This man has the listed risk factors, prior vancomycin and cephalosporins and a long ICU stay, and his E. faecium has a very high vancomycin MIC. The altered terminal residue explains the failure.
why: Vancomycin is a glycopeptide, not a beta-lactam, so beta-lactamases do not affect it.
PBP2a is the MRSA beta-lactam mechanism, and vancomycin does not bind PBPs.
Aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes act on aminoglycosides, not on vancomycin.
Enterococci are Gram-positive and have no outer membrane porins.
explain.takeaway: VRE (mostly E. faecium) replace D-Ala-D-Ala with D-Ala-D-Lac in peptidoglycan precursors, lowering vancomycin binding about 1,000-fold.

questions.stem:
A 47-year-old man with extensive burns in the intensive care unit develops ventilator-associated pneumonia. Cultures grow a non-motile, aerobic, oxidase-negative Gram-negative coccobacillus that persisted on bed rails despite routine disinfectant cleaning. The isolate is resistant to gentamicin and tobramycin. Analysis of the drug recovered from the culture shows that the gentamicin molecules have acquired acetyl and phosphate groups.

Which statement about this resistance is correct?
choices: It is caused by mutation of the 30S subunit so the drug cannot bind
It is the main mode of aminoglycoside resistance in this organism
It is caused by D-alanyl-D-lactate precursors in the cell wall
It is intrinsic, because aerobes cannot take up aminoglycosides
It can be reversed by adding clavulanic acid to the aminoglycoside

explain.html:
A. baumannii is a non-motile, aerobic, oxidase-negative Gram-negative coccobacillus that survives dry and moist surfaces and common disinfectants, causing ventilator-associated pneumonia and burn infections. It resists aminoglycosides in several ways, and the main mode is aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes (AMEs). AMEs are acetyltransferases, phosphotransferases and adenyltransferases that chemically add groups to the drug, and they are often carried on transposable elements. Efflux pumps and rRNA-modifying enzymes are other mechanisms.

The decisive finding is that the recovered gentamicin itself now carries acetyl and phosphate groups: the drug was modified, not the ribosome. In a burn-unit VAP from an organism that persisted on bed rails, that is AME-mediated resistance in A. baumannii. Future drugs may aim to inhibit AMEs.
why: Ribosomal (rRNA) modification exists, but here the drug itself was chemically changed.
D-Ala-D-Lac precursors are the vancomycin resistance mechanism, unrelated to aminoglycosides.
Intrinsic aminoglycoside resistance belongs to anaerobes, and this is an aerobe that acquired enzymes.
Clavulanic acid inhibits beta-lactamases and has no effect on aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes.
explain.takeaway: Aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes (acetyl-, phospho- and adenyltransferases) are the main mode of aminoglycoside resistance in MDR Acinetobacter baumannii.

questions.stem:
A 70-year-old man with COPD and diabetes has been in the intensive care unit for 2 weeks with a central line and urinary catheter. He develops fever and hypotension. A prior culture grew a motile, oxidase-positive, non-lactose-fermenting Gram-negative rod that made a blue-green pigment and resisted several drug classes. Cultures are pending, and the team must start empiric therapy now.

Which empiric approach does the lecture recommend for this high-risk patient?
choices: Two drugs from different classes, each with activity against Pseudomonas
A single carbapenem, since it covers every Gram-negative rod
Vancomycin plus daptomycin to cover any resistant organism
Ceftriaxone plus metronidazole for Gram-negatives and anaerobes
Tigecycline alone, as the last-option agent for MDR rods

explain.html:
P. aeruginosa is a motile, aerobic, oxidase-positive, non-lactose-fermenting Gram-negative rod that makes pyocyanin (blue-green) and is a leading cause of hospital infections. MDR strains use the same mechanisms as MDR Acinetobacter: beta-lactamases, AMEs, efflux, porin loss and target changes. Risk factors include a prolonged ICU stay, invasive devices, underlying disease such as diabetes and COPD and older age. High-risk patients should be treated empirically with two different drug classes that both cover Pseudomonas, for example an aminoglycoside plus piperacillin-tazobactam.

This man has every risk factor and a prior resistant blue-green isolate, and he is septic before cultures return. Two antipseudomonal classes raise the chance that at least one works while susceptibilities are pending. Narrow therapy once the results are back.
why: MDR Pseudomonas can be carbapenem resistant, so one agent alone risks failure in a high-risk patient.
Vancomycin cannot penetrate Gram-negatives, and daptomycin is a Gram-positive drug, so neither covers Pseudomonas.
This pair is not the two-antipseudomonal-class regimen recommended, and metronidazole adds only anaerobic coverage.
Tigecycline is the last-option drug for carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter, not an antipseudomonal agent, and monotherapy breaks the two-class rule.
explain.takeaway: High-risk patients with possible MDR Pseudomonas are treated empirically with two antipseudomonal drugs from different classes, such as an aminoglycoside plus piperacillin-tazobactam.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Know how to treat each resistant infection (responsible for drugs highlighted in red).
